paragraphs.heading: When life crashes
paragraphs.text: A mass extinction, also called an extinction event or biotic crisis, is a fast and widespread drop in the variety of life on Earth. Scientists spot one as a steep fall in both the variety and the numbers of multicellular living things. It happens when species are dying out faster than the background extinction rate and faster than new species are appearing.

paragraphs.heading: How many big ones
paragraphs.text: Counts of major mass extinctions over the last 540 million years run from as few as five to more than twenty. The numbers differ because researchers disagree on what counts as major and on which data best measure past diversity. In a landmark 1982 paper, Jack Sepkoski and David M. Raup picked out five stretches of time with unusually heavy losses. Later, stricter statistics confirmed that animal life in the current eon, the Phanerozoic, has been through at least five major mass extinctions and many minor ones. Even so, these "Big Five" seem to be the largest members of a fairly smooth range of events rather than a separate class.

paragraphs.heading: Ice and thaw in the Ordovician
paragraphs.text: The Late Ordovician mass extinction probably came in two pulses near the boundary between the Ordovician and Silurian periods. The first pulse matched a cooling and a large glaciation in the south, and the second matched the thaw. Together they killed 27% of all families, 57% of all genera and 85% of all species, which leads many scientists to rank it second of the five by share of genera lost. Its cause is still argued over: studies in 2020 pointed to warming linked to volcanism and to a lack of oxygen, while many earlier studies named global cooling as the main driver, at least of the first pulse.

paragraphs.heading: Oceans without oxygen
paragraphs.text: The Late Devonian held two major extinction events, and both have been linked to anoxic events, times when seawater lost its oxygen on a global scale. The larger, the Kellwasser Event about 372 million years ago, destroyed coral reefs and many tropical animals of the seabed, including jawless fish, brachiopods and trilobites. Many scientists think rivers washed nutrients from the land into the ocean and fed enormous algal blooms. When the algae died and rotted, they used up the oxygen dissolved in the water, and this anoxia finally caused the die-off. The second, the Hangenberg Event about 359 million years ago, closed the Devonian, ending the armored placoderm fish and nearly ending the newly evolved ammonoids.

paragraphs.heading: The Great Dying
paragraphs.text: The End Permian extinction, known as the Great Dying, struck at the turn from the Permian to the Triassic. It was the largest extinction of the Phanerozoic: about 81% of marine species vanished, along with an estimated 70% of land vertebrate species. It is also the largest known extinction of insects. The trilobites disappeared for good, as did major coral groups such as the rugosans and tabulates. Vertebrates took 30 million years to recover, but the empty niches gave archosaurs, the relatives of dinosaurs and crocodiles, room to spread.

paragraphs.heading: Was land spared
paragraphs.text: New work suggests the Great Dying may have hit land less hard than once thought. Fossil pollen and spores show that some plant communities were barely or only briefly disturbed. A 2025 study in what is now China found a thriving ecosystem only 75,000 years after the event, pointing to a quicker recovery. Some scientists go further and argue there may have been no mass extinction on land at all, citing evidence from plants, insects and four-limbed vertebrates.
